blogs.description: dbreunig/nesformer Inspired by qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502…
blogs.content:
dbreunig/nesformer

Inspired by qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. You can now play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros (very slowly) running inside Qwen!

 In a comment on Hacker News Drew reveals the Opus 5.5 prompts he used to build this system:

 Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed.

 Followed by:

 I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM.

 Apparently Opus found and then used this collection of conformance tests for the NES CPU released 15 years ago by Christopher Pow.

 Via Hacker News

 Tags: games , ai , generative-ai , llms , drew-breunig , qwen , conformance-suites

If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing. Document why, share it with your community of peers, bring it to your manager, and work to find solutions. An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.

 — Terk Terkowitz , An update from Amazon engineering leadership on the role of the developer in the age of AI

blogs.content:
(Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images)

 Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!

 As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings .

 On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week.

 Finally, Some Anthropic Numbers.  Monday morning brought us Anthropic’s S-1, and not a moment too soon. After four years of arguments about the economics at frontier labs, we now have some real numbers to sink our teeth into, and Ben did just that with his Update on Tuesday . Come for that analysis, and then head over to this week’s Sharp Tech where we talked in depth about what Anthropic is telling investors, questions that remain unanswered, plus why the SEC forced Anthropic to help us understand Meta’s Muse bet . — Andrew Sharp

 The End of the Internet as We Know It (and I Feel Fine) . Arriving on the heels of a handful of ominous cybersecurity incidents and with continued upheaval guaranteed, Monday’s Article made two distinct predictions . First, the pressure applied by AI will eventually (or imminently?) rupture the global internet that we’ve come to know for the past 25 years. But second, as society moves to more localized solutions and products, that may in fact be a welcome development for all of us who have come to accept degraded experiences throughout our technological lives. As an avid group chatter who’s more or less abandoned public social media, I can certainly get behind the second take!  — AS

 Autocracies Then and Now. On Sharp China this week, we began with an extended look at the climate of fear across the Chinese bureaucracy as Xi Jinping continues an anti-corruption crackdown that was absolutely necessary but may be going further than Xi’s earlier proponents ever expected. Then, we turn to a glorious mess surrounding Mao Zedong and international soccer star Kylian Mbappé. On both that episode and in this week’s Sharp Text , I make the point that connipitions like this one, anchored in a bizarre debate over Mao’s governing history, are evidence that rumors of a Chinese century have been greatly exaggerated.  — AS

---

 Presented by

 When I write about tech companies, I am often writing about businesses that depend on Stripe , because Stripe provides the foundation for Internet-native companies — including Stratechery.

 Consider Substack: building Stratechery was complicated and involved gluing together disparate pieces; Substack made it easy by delivering an integrated offering. One piece that was the same, however, was Stripe: Substack creators are also Stripe customers, as are creators on many other platforms.

 Zoom out and the pattern repeats. Fintechs can build entire business models around card programs without ever having to build the issuing and processing infrastructure underneath it.

AI companies can charge for what customers actually use, which is particularly important when usage also drives costs, without having to build the systems to track and bill for it themselves.

 No business succeeds because of Stripe. Stripe doesn’t answer the hard questions about what to build or whether anyone will actually use it. But it does make more things practical to try.

---

 Stratechery Articles and Updates

 The End of the Internet — The old Internet, where anyone could host a server is over, but it’s just the final blow in an ending that has been coming for years. The future, though, is brighter than it appears.

 Meta Earnings, Muse and the Frontier, Musebook — Meta’s earnings come in the context of Zuckerberg delivering on his promise; if investors believe in Muse they must support Meta’s spending on compute.

blogs.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,617 new readers. Nvidia’s chips are at the center of the U.S.-China AI race, and Washington has spent years trying to keep the best ones out of Beijing’s hands.
 Now, a New York Times report says U.S. intelligence found that an alleged Chinese asset had built close ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang… and the White House chose not to act.

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 Report: Nvidia CEO targeted by alleged Chinese spy

 Rowan’s Corner: ‘Sent from my agent’

 Make ElevenLabs voiceovers sound more natural

 Anthropic’s AI now monitors its own conversations

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 NVIDIA
 🕵️  Report: Nvidia CEO targeted by alleged Chinese spy
 Image source: Net Thunder on LinkedIn

 The Rundown: The NYT just reported that U.S. officials found Alice Huang, an exec at Singapore-based data center firm Megaspeed, was allegedly passing intelligence to Beijing while keeping close ties with Jensen Huang, with Trump briefed about a year ago.
 The details:
 It’s unclear what Ms. Huang passed to Beijing or its value, but officials worried she could offer insight into Trump’s view on chip sales to China, and into Nvidia itself.

 Officials didn’t believe Jensen knew of her alleged role when Trump was briefed; he never got a defensive briefing, often given to U.S. citizens targeted by spies.

 Megaspeed, already under U.S. probe for steering Nvidia chips to China, bought at least $4.8B in Nvidia gear via a sister firm, and remains an Nvidia cloud partner.

 Nvidia called Jensen’s meetings with Ms. Huang routine, saying customers get ordinary business info and “zero information relevant to national security.”

 Megaspeed said outside counsel is investigating and it’s cooperating with the U.S., while China called the claims “groundless smears and slanders.”

 Why it matters: The report reads like a spy thriller, but nothing has been publicly proven, including whether Ms. Huang passed anything to China. The immediate fallout may hit the loophole allowing firms like Megaspeed to rent Nvidia-powered computing from Southeast Asia to Chinese AI labs — one Trump reopened but may now close.

 TOGETHER WITH OPENART
 🧑‍🎨  Create a launch video for your business  

 The Rundown: Need a launch video for your business? Simply paste your website link, add your brand assets, and define your target audience. OpenArt’s AI video agent will shape the story and messaging while handling the script, motion design, voiceover, and video editing.
 With OpenArt, you can:
 Turn your website, screenshots, or pitch deck into a launch video

 Create short promos or longer videos to showcase your business

 Refine scenes, voiceovers, or music by describing the changes

 Go beyond launches with product ads and UGC-style videos

 Create your launch video with OpenArt .

 ROWAN’S CORNER
 🤖  ‘Sent from my agent’
 h/t to @gregisenberg for the tweet

 Rowan: “Sent from my agent” is becoming the new “Sent from iPhone.” That’s a tweet my friend Greg Isenberg recently made that’s stirring up conversation.
 Basically, “Sent from my iPhone” started as a way to buy forgiveness for typos and messy formatting when emailing someone from your iPhone. But when someone sees “Sent from my agent,” the real message they receive is: you weren’t worth my attention .
 There’s real tension here (for me included). Agents are the biggest leverage available right now, and I run several tasks through them, saving me at least a few hours a week. But I also believe going the extra mile and writing something yourself shows the other human respect.
 So here’s my line:
 Anything that touches a person is me — social posts, messages, recruiting calls, live video.

 Anything that’s a task, an agent can do.

 I also have a growing thesis that real human relationships will only become more valuable as AI gets better. Anything that risks that trust is probably a bad trade. Personally, if I see “sent from my agent,” I’m deleting the email.
 I’ve written before that AI intuition is the most important skill of this decade, knowing which tasks to hand to AI, and this is the perfect example. Use agents everywhere, except on people.
 Are you using agents to respond to your emails, or do you think the human touch shows respect? Let me know in the poll at the bottom of the email. I’m curious!

 AI TRAINING
 🎙️  Make ElevenLabs voiceovers sound more natural

 The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll add Audio Tags to a short Eleven v4 voiceover, compare it with the plain version, and create a short scene with two speakers.
 Step-by-step:
 Open ElevenLabs Text to Speech, choose one voice, and select Eleven v4. Generate the guide’s plain script and save it for comparison

 Paste the tagged version without changing the spoken words. Keep the same voice and settings so you can hear the difference

 Compare the opening, pace, and final line. If the delivery stays flat, make one cue more specific. Change one thing at a time

 If a tag gets read aloud, check the model and square brackets. Keep the direction short and place it before the words it should affect

 Open Dialogue mode, add two voices, and generate the guide’s exchange. Check the words, speakers, and timing before downloading the clips

 Pro tip: Save a plain version before adding tags. A more expressive read may still sound less natural. You can find our full cheat sheet, annotated scripts, and review checklist here .

 PRESENTED BY GLEAN
 🚀  From data to decisions, faster

 The Rundown: Business data spans across apps, warehouses, and BI platforms, while the context behind the numbers lives in documents, tickets, and conversations. Glean’s upcoming webinar helps you bring it all together, find trusted answers, and make data-driven decisions without SQL or a BI background.
 In this webinar, you’ll learn how to:
 Query business data in natural language

 Quickly build dashboards to track key metrics

 Connect metrics with enterprise context

 Register for the webinar and put AI to work .

 ANTHROPIC / AI SAFETY
 🚨  Anthropic’s AI now monitors its own conversations
 Image source: Anthropic

 The Rundown: Anthropic introduced “self-assessment,” a technique where Claude reviews the chat after each reply and flags potential misuse, saying the system has been active since June and catching large-scale abuse that might otherwise be missed.
 The details:
 Claude gives each conversation a quick safety verdict (whether it’s harmful, what kind of harm, and how urgent), which helps prioritize cases for human review.

 On Claude Fable 5, it catches 78% of potentially harmful conversations flagged by a stronger classifier, and 94% of high-priority ones, at a 1% false-positive rate.

 It helped uncover 100K+ child-abuse flags from a single API customer, reported to authorities, plus an automated romance-scam operation run through Claude Code.

 Anthropic admits it’s weak as a lone blocker, cutting attack success in red-team tests only from 79% to 54%, though it made each successful attack cost ~4x more.

 Why it matters: After Anthropic’s own reports showed Claude being misused for cyberattacks and weapons work, letting the AI check and flag misuse in its own chats is a welcome layer. Claude brings everything it understands to each judgment, but it can also share the same blind spots, meaning the system isn’t foolproof (yet!).

 QUICK HITS

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY
 ▸ Michael used Claude Cowork to build a 3D home design app
 Today’s workflow comes from reader Michael Saif :
 “I built this web app for a friend who is building a house. It lets you see the finished version of every room in the planned home before anything is built. I described the idea to Claude Cowork, had a short back-and-forth answering its questions, and it built the app in four stages. You can upload one or more floor plans, select a room, and view it from several rotatable 3D angles.
 You can then describe how you want the room to look when completed, such as ‘Show me with a dark-colored wood floor with blue walls,’ and ask for changes, like light-colored wood floors. You can also add furniture to see how the room will look when finished, save multiple designs for each room, and export any image as a PNG. The whole build took less than an hour from start to finish.”

blogs.name: Tomasz Tunguz
blogs.title: Crossing the Trillion Dollar Chasm
blogs.description: Who will be the first $10t company? The one that first crosses the trillion dollar chasm : building a $1t AI compute engine before AI erodes…
blogs.content:
Who will be the first $10t company? The one that first crosses the trillion dollar chasm : building a $1t AI compute engine before AI erodes the legacy cash cow paying for the GPUs.

 In the last few weeks, two CEOs have put a $1t revenue target on their businesses : Andy Jassy & Elon Musk. We are tracking each company’s cloud & AI compute engine toward $1t in annualized segment revenue 1 .

 Andy Jassy, President & CEO of Amazon 2 :

 “We believe that AWS can grow north of 40% in each of 2027 & in 2028, & be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next 5 to 10 years.”

 Elon Musk, on SpaceX’s Q3 call 3 :

 “SpaceX could reach a $500b to $1t annual recurring revenue run rate by 2027.”

 Meanwhile, growth rates are accelerating at every hyperscaler on businesses generating $30b to $50b per quarter 4 .

 Assume current growth rates with a 15% annual decay & Andy Jassy’s guided 40%+ growth in 2027 & 2028 5 . Google Cloud overtakes Azure in mid-2027 & passes AWS by the end of 2027 to become the largest of the three cloud businesses 6 .

 On that trajectory, Google Cloud & SpaceX both cross $250b in quarterly revenue ($1t annualized run rate) in 2030 & AWS follows in 2032 : provided power, silicon & balance sheets hold.

 Why did the market sell off two of the three hyperscalers on earnings day? Investors are worried that the legacy businesses will not be able to sustain the positive cash flows to continue the capex spend in sufficient time to realize the ROI 7 .

 Philipp Schindler, SVP & Chief Business Officer of Google 8 :

 “Look, in Q3, Search grew 12% year-over-year to $63b… it’s worth noting that the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode.”

 Alphabet’s search queries & visual searches are at record highs, with AI Mode queries running 3x the length of traditional searches, but Search & other advertising growth slowed to 12% ($63.3b), down from 19% in Q1 & 17% in Q2, as AI Mode monetizes at a lower rate than classic ten-blue-link search 8 .

 Amazon’s retail & advertising machine faces the same question : whether external shopping agents bypass the search results pages where Amazon Ads generates $19.6b per quarter (up 12% in Q3, down from 26% in Q2).

 Andy Jassy, President & CEO of Amazon 2 :

 “The natural question is whether agentic shopping from external horizontal agents is meaningfully impacting Amazon Ads, & the answer is no. Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet, as the experience is still not great nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly to research or one-click order there.”

 Primarily Google & Amazon must cross a new chasm : refocusing capital & product around hardware, gigawatts & agentic compute while their historical cash cows absorb the shock of AI.

 Microsoft is the only hyperscaler whose legacy enterprise franchise is expanding ARPU through AI faster than seat growth is slowing 9 . ServiceNow is seeing the opposite : its market cap fell 29% on fears of AI erosion of its core seat-based business 10 .

 Google must prove that three-times-longer AI queries & autonomous shopping agents can monetize at the same yield as ten blue links. The first $10t company will be the one whose new compute engine reaches $1t before its old monopoly pays the tab.

---

 Segment versus consolidated scope : Jassy’s $1t target applies to AWS segment revenue ($46.0b in Q3 2026, or $184b annualized), whereas Amazon consolidated revenue is already $201.9b per quarter ($808b annualized, mostly retail at a lower multiple). Musk’s $500b to $1t target applies to SpaceX consolidated revenue ($14.6b in Q3 2026, led by $7.6b in Super Intelligence). Assuming a 10x revenue multiple on cloud & AI compute, crossing $1t in annualized segment revenue supports a $10t standalone valuation.  ↩︎

 Amazon Q3 2026 earnings release & conference call (October 29, 2026). Consolidated revenue was $201.9b (+12% YoY). AWS Q3 2026 revenue was $45.98b (+39.3% YoY) with $17.77b in operating income (38.7% margin) & $578b in backlog. Amazon Ads revenue was $19.6b (+12% YoY, down from +26% in Q2 2026 & +22% in Q1 2026).  ↩︎   ↩︎

 SpaceX Q3 2026 earnings release & conference call (October 20, 2026). Q3 2026 consolidated revenue was $14.58b (+161% YoY) : Super Intelligence (SI : xAI, Grok, cloud compute agreements & Cursor) generated $7.56b (+830% YoY), Connectivity (Starlink) generated $5.25b (+69% YoY) & Space (Launch) generated $1.77b (+6% YoY). Reaching $500b to $1t of AI ARR at current monetization (about $17.8b annualized AI revenue per gw on 1.7gw of live compute at Q3 end) requires 28gw to 56gw of live compute, whereas Q3 capex of $19.59b (roughly $78b/year pace at $38b per gw all-in) funds roughly 2gw per year.  ↩︎

 In Q3 2026, Google Cloud more than doubled year over year, surging 103% to $30.7b as first-party model APIs reached 32b tokens per minute & Cloud backlog hit $561b. Azure grew 48% to $33.2b inside a $63.9b Microsoft Cloud quarter, with Q2 guidance pointing to 49% to 50% constant-currency growth. AWS accelerated to 39% growth at $46.0b ($184b annualized run rate), its fastest pace since Q4 2021, & SpaceX grew total revenue 161% year over year to $14.6b, led by its Super Intelligence segment, which rose 830% to $7.6b.  ↩︎

 Calculation : Projected Q3 quarterly revenue starts from Q3 2026 actuals (Google Cloud $30.7b at 103.0% YoY, Azure $33.2b at 48.0% YoY, AWS $46.0b at 39.3% YoY & SpaceX $14.6b at 161.4% YoY) & compounds forward assuming each year’s YoY growth rate declines by 15% (g_{t+1} = 0.85 * g_t). A standard 25% decay curve would be too conservative for AWS & Azure because both are guided to compound near 40% to 50% per year : for Andy Jassy’s prediction to hold, AWS must defy normal large-law deceleration by holding 40%+ growth through 2027 & 2028 on a $184b run-rate base, converting its $578b backlog as fast as it lands power & silicon, & decaying no faster than 15% per year thereafter to cross $250b per quarter ($1t annualized run rate) in 2032.  ↩︎

 Segment definitions across the cloud businesses include hardware sales as well as rental : Alphabet CFO Anat Ashkenazi noted on the Q3 2026 call that Google Cloud’s 103% growth ($30.71b) & Alphabet’s 32% jump in other cost of revenues ($35.1b) were “driven by hardware costs, primarily related to the sales of TPU systems,” alongside AI infrastructure rental & Google Workspace.  ↩︎

 Post-earnings stock price reaction following Q3 2026 earnings releases (October 28 to 30, 2026) : Microsoft -0.2% (0%), Amazon -12.0% in after-hours trading following its Q3 release & Alphabet -12.6% (-13%) on October 29.  ↩︎

 Alphabet Q3 2026 earnings release & conference call (October 28, 2026). Consolidated revenue was $127.6b (+25% YoY). Google Search & other advertising revenue grew 12% YoY to $63.35b in Q3 2026, decelerating from 19% YoY growth in Q1 2026 ($60.40b) & 17% YoY growth in Q2 2026 ($63.27b), & rising just $79m (+0.1%) sequentially from Q2 to Q3 despite Sundar Pichai noting that “our year-over-year query growth rate is the highest it’s been in the last five years.”  ↩︎   ↩︎

 Microsoft FY27 Q1 (calendar Q3 2026) earnings release, Form 8-K & conference call (October 28, 2026) : Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud revenue grew 17% reported (+18% in constant currency; +19% adjusted CC), with ARPU expansion across M365 Copilot, E5, the new E7 bundle (which reached millions of paid seats) & GitHub Copilot more than offsetting a slowdown in paid M365 commercial seat growth to 5% on softer E3 & standalone SKU execution. That enterprise cash engine kept Microsoft at +$18.63b in Q3 free cash flow on $45.2b of capex (including finance leases), whereas Alphabet swung to -$9.07b in Q3 free cash flow on $51.36b of capex ($195b to $205b full-year 2026 guide) & Amazon reported -$42.4b in trailing-twelve-month free cash flow on $77.3b of Q3 capex ($220b full-year 2026 guide).  ↩︎

 ServiceNow Q3 2026 earnings release & post-earnings trading (October 28 to 30, 2026) : shares fell from $150.13 at the October 28 close to $105.65 on October 30 (-29.6%) despite 20.5% constant-currency Q3 subscription revenue growth ($3.988b), as Q4 cRPO guidance decelerated to 18.5% constant currency & investors scrutinized seat-based software pricing in an agentic world.  ↩︎

Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!

As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings .

On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week.

Finally, Some Anthropic Numbers.  Monday morning brought us Anthropic’s S-1, and not a moment too soon. After four years of arguments about the economics at frontier labs, we now have some real numbers to sink our teeth into, and Ben did just that with his Update on Tuesday . Come for that analysis, and then head over to this week’s Sharp Tech where we talked in depth about what Anthropic is telling investors, questions that remain unanswered, plus why the SEC forced Anthropic to help us understand Meta’s Muse bet . — Andrew Sharp

The End of the Internet as We Know It (and I Feel Fine) . Arriving on the heels of a handful of ominous cybersecurity incidents and with continued upheaval guaranteed, Monday’s Article made two distinct predictions . First, the pressure applied by AI will eventually (or imminently?) rupture the global internet that we’ve come to know for the past 25 years. But second, as society moves to more localized solutions and products, that may in fact be a welcome development for all of us who have come to accept degraded experiences throughout our technological lives. As an avid group chatter who’s more or less abandoned public social media, I can certainly get behind the second take!  — AS

Autocracies Then and Now. On Sharp China this week, we began with an extended look at the climate of fear across the Chinese bureaucracy as Xi Jinping continues an anti-corruption crackdown that was absolutely necessary but may be going further than Xi’s earlier proponents ever expected. Then, we turn to a glorious mess surrounding Mao Zedong and international soccer star Kylian Mbappé. On both that episode and in this week’s Sharp Text , I make the point that connipitions like this one, anchored in a bizarre debate over Mao’s governing history, are evidence that rumors of a Chinese century have been greatly exaggerated.  — AS

---

Presented by

When I write about tech companies, I am often writing about businesses that depend on Stripe , because Stripe provides the foundation for Internet-native companies — including Stratechery.

Consider Substack: building Stratechery was complicated and involved gluing together disparate pieces; Substack made it easy by delivering an integrated offering. One piece that was the same, however, was Stripe: Substack creators are also Stripe customers, as are creators on many other platforms.

Zoom out and the pattern repeats. Fintechs can build entire business models around card programs without ever having to build the issuing and processing infrastructure underneath it.

AI companies can charge for what customers actually use, which is particularly important when usage also drives costs, without having to build the systems to track and bill for it themselves.

No business succeeds because of Stripe. Stripe doesn’t answer the hard questions about what to build or whether anyone will actually use it. But it does make more things practical to try.

blogs.title: An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: An interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar about AI diffusion and safety, forward-deployed engineer, and what the battle in tech is actually about.
blogs.content:
An interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar about AI diffusion and safety, forward-deployed engineer, and what the battle in tech is actually about.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

Today’s Stratechery Interview is with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar . Sankar has worked at Palantir for 20 years, and has taken on an increasingly visible role as public intellectual, including authoring the book Mobilize , an exhortation “To Reboot the American Industrial Base and Stop World War III”. I previously interviewed Sankar in June 2023 . That interview is a great place to start in terms of understanding Palantir, which we mostly discuss in this interview in the context of AI.

To that end, in this interview we discuss why Sankar thinks the industry is insufficiently focused on AI diffusion, why companies focused on the top-line have more success adopting AI, and why he is frustrated at the labs refusal to take a systems engineering approach to AI safety. Then we discuss what Palantir has learned from AI, how companies can preserve alpha instead of the median, and whether or not we need more models. Sankar also explains exactly what a forward-deployed engineer is, why tech is in a religious war, and his retrospective on Anthropic’s battle with the U.S. government.

This Interview is presented by Stripe, the economic infrastructure of AI, and for Stratechery itself.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War

This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

Topics:

Diffusing Intelligence | Top Line vs. Bottom Line | Safety and Systems Engineering | Palantir’s AI Lessons | Alpha vs. Beta | Model Questions | Forward-Deployed Engineering | Anthropic vs. the U.S. Government | AI Religion

Background

Shyam Sankar, welcome back to Stratechery.

SS: Ben, thanks for having me back.

Well, the last time we talked was in conjunction with Ted Mabrey , the head of Palantir Commercial. As is usually the case with dual interviews, we got right down to business — and I do have to say, I do a lot of interviews where I usually kind of know where I want to go, but that one was super helpful to me in understanding Palantir and thinking about AI generally . But before we get into that, we never got to do my traditional background questions — where you came from, how you got to where you are. So for you, do we start in Orlando, in Lagos, or in India?

SS: At least Lagos. My father, in his early 20s, moved to Lagos and built one of the first pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities in all of Africa. He set up this whole life there for the better part of ten years. I was born in India, but really I grew up until I was three in Lagos.

And then there was this horrible armed robbery that happened at the house — they decapitated the dog, pistol-whipped my father, and threatened my mother. So we left all of our earthly possessions behind and started over again in Orlando, which ended up being a truly phenomenal place to grow up. The profound optimism of Disney World, the shadow of the Space Coast , seeing shuttle launches in elementary school, running into your courtyard filled with this sense of optimism about how technology will inevitably lead to a better world — which, if you fast-forward twenty years from the ’80s, I think kids were fed a very different diet of Terminator and “ nature always finds a way “, “How dare man try to do anything that creates progress?”, so that’s really where it started.

Is that actually the ultimate example of man overcoming nature — not the space shuttle, but in fact Disney World?

SS: (laughing) That’s true! The fact that millions of people go there every year, to the middle of the swamp — and it’s fantastic, a lot of fun.

What does meritocracy mean to you? I was reading the recent profile of you in Colossus , and it opened with [Palantir CEO] Alex Karp’s statements in that regard, but it was put in the context of you growing up in Orlando, taking an entrance exam to go to Trinity High School, and how that launched you into what you became. Is that a sentiment from Alex, is it from you, or what’s your take?

SS: It’s a sentiment for both of us, for different reasons. We’re both kind of acquired tastes, in many ways, and living in a world that judges you by the fruits you bear, rather than any dimension you have no control over, is obviously a better world to live in. I think it’s a precondition to the American Dream.

I was going to ask you that. Because you have this background — born in India, originally living in Lagos, come to America. What does being an American mean to you? Is that the same question, or is there some tension between those two things?

SS: They overlap profoundly. Being an American is this profound belief in your own human agency, and the community you’re in, and the ability to create a more perfect union — the recognition, the ability to hold the contradiction, that not everything is perfect today but it’s incumbent on us to make it better. That may sound a little Pollyannish and even corny, but that doesn’t exist anywhere else. Everywhere else, people are profoundly cynical — things are the way they are — and there’s a very thin line between cynicism and nihilism, and you kind of give up on everything. That’s the death spiral, that’s how you get the Dark Ages.

After university and graduate school, you worked on Xoom, on remittances — and then you go to work for Palantir.

SS: Xoom with an X.

Xoom with an X, that’s right. Not the Zoom with a Z — which maybe I shouldn’t be talking to, since you’re now an executive at Palantir using Zoom with a Z, but that’s another discussion. You worked on Xoom and remittances, then Palantir, working on national security, arguing for building our homegrown industrial base. There’s an argument there that — to take a paradox that’s maybe unfair — how do you go from a career focused on sending money out of America to being an advocate for money here in America, rebuilding our capital base? Is there tension there, or am I creating paradoxes out of thin air to build a theme?

SS: I think you’re creating a bit of a paradox out of thin air. First of all, there’s a policy question — if you have a working class trying to get money to support their family, how can they do that as efficiently as possible?

The bigger issue is the profound lie of globalization. The calculus that globalization got wrong is this idea that we can do the innovation and “they” can do the production — “they” make the things, we do the innovation. The problem is that innovation is a consequence of productivity, if you stop making the thing, you cede the stimulus required to do the innovation around the thing.

The example I always give young computer scientists is, what do you think motivated Google to do the research behind “ Attention Is All You Need “? If you talk to that team, they wanted the 3% improvement in Google Translate. You cannot think of something more prosaic leading to something more profound. So we should be very careful where we give up — we buy a little too much into comparative advantage and give up the stimulus for production.

Why do you think — what leads to that mistake of thinking that it’s okay to just own the inputs and not worry about the outputs?

SS: Because at the margin, it’s true. At the margin, you can hire WuXi as a cheap set of hands at the lab bench to do a little bit of work. But at the limit, that’s a transfer of knowledge. At every increment it seems to make sense — you’re still doing the innovation — until one day you wake up and realize, “Oh, I don’t have it anymore”.

Diffusing Intelligence

You’re the only Stratechery interview that I’ve offered a job to. You sent over a list of questions you wanted me to talk about, and I have to say they’re really good — I did ask if you wanted to prepare all my interviews going forward, I don’t think I got a response, maybe the email got lost.

SS: (laughing) I’m thinking about it.

Okay, good. Well, let’s drill in — we’ll take your outline, why not, go through it and talk about it, and I think there are themes that might emerge. So number one, and this is from Shyam Sankar, does this count as a Shyam bomb, by the way, the long extended email detailing what we should talk about?

SS: It’s not nearly vitriolic enough, so you’re spared.

Got it, that makes sense. Number one, is the AI industry solving the wrong bottleneck? You argue we are over-investing intellectually in the supply of intelligence and under-investing in diffusion. Tell me what you mean.

SS: If you thought about a crass metaphor of AI through electricity — there are people who generate the electrons, the power producers — for electricity to have any impact on our economy, there needed to be other people who built machine tools that run on those electrons. And that led to a profound revolution. Not only would you introduce one piece of machinery into your factory, you’d start redesigning your factories around the fact that we have electrons.

Let’s call that diffusion, how does the miracle of electricity diffuse into the economy? There’s a similar question with AI. I think we are very focused on how to make better models, smarter models, more machine intelligence — and we should keep doing that — but we’re very under-indexed on how to accelerate the rate of diffusion. Where is the economic value being created? How do we turn these tokens into economic value more quickly with a great ratio around it? I’m obsessed with that, because I think there’s a license to operate in society where the benefits of this stuff diffusing really do matter and I think we’re getting the calculus around some of this pretty wrong.

So who is “we”? Who are the ones insufficiently focused on diffusion? Who are you trying to convince here?

SS: I think the labs are, but in general the entire market structure. People are being rewarded — and it’s very rational, if you’re a lab, you’ve been in your own reinforcement-learning loop, you do fundamental research, you make a more powerful model, and your valuation doubles or quadruples and every year it seems to keep working. Baked into that is the idea that eventually this stuff will diffuse, eventually there will be economic value.

But one of the conceits I’m not sure people are getting right is, what is the atomic unit of the enterprise? Let’s leave consumer out of this. The presumption, as expressed through the product strategy you see from the labs, is that the atomic unit of the enterprise is the knowledge worker — if I can make every worker more productive, that’s the ROI, and that’s not actually true. The atomic unit of the enterprise is the workflow, you can make a single supply-chain analyst more productive and generate no incremental ROI, you have to make the entire supply-chain workflow measurably more productive to capture the value.

There are some roles where the cardinality collapses — the knowledge worker is the workflow, like coding — so you have perfect product-market fit for those things, and you can chase unbounded productivity. But that’s a very small part of everything we do in the real economy.

Again, I don’t understand the audience here. In a market, shouldn’t the model makers just do their job, which is making better models, and then there are lots of opportunities for companies to take those models and diffuse them? Isn’t that what Palantir is trying to do? Who is the target of this exhortation?

SS: To those wondering, “Okay, we’re creating this, we’re spending trillions of dollars, where’s the return, how’s it working, why is the best example of excellence an AI assistant, which is nice and convenient but that’s not going to inflect our GDP?”. You think the big problems that I’m interested in solving — I...

blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: Meta's earnings come in the context of Zuckerberg delivering on his promise; if investors believe in Muse they must support Meta's spending on compute.
blogs.content:
Meta's earnings come in the context of Zuckerberg delivering on his promise; if investors believe in Muse they must support Meta's spending on compute.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

I joined Myke Hurley on the Cortex Podcast to discuss how I write Stratechery. Then, I joined John Collison on Cheeky Pint to ( again ) interview United CEO Scott Kirby . Both podcasts were recorded a couple of weeks ago but just posted in the last few days.

On to the Update:

Meta Earnings

From Bloomberg :

Meta Platforms Inc. shares fell after Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg told investors the company would bet even more aggressively on artificial intelligence. During its quarterly earnings report Wednesday, the social-media giant boosted its capital spending plans for the year and announced a new class of nonvoting stock that could ultimately be used to help pay for acquisitions and other expenses. The moves show that Meta has confidence that its already-stratospheric spending on AI is bearing fruit. After struggling to persuade investors to accept ballooning costs, Meta has made headway with its technology in recent months, especially with a new AI agent called Muse. Zuckerberg pointed to that progress as reason to keep plowing ahead.

Meta is indeed plowing ahead; from the Wall Street Journal earlier this week:

Meta Platforms unveiled a plan to raise up to $95 billion in waves of stock offerings, as the company embarks on a cash-raising spree to fund its massive investments in artificial-intelligence infrastructure. The Facebook parent said Monday it will launch roughly $35 billion in public offerings, comprising $22.5 billion of Class A common stock and $12.5 billion of depositary shares representing mandatory convertible preferred stock.

Meta also plans to establish an at-the-market stock offering program of up to $60 billion, potentially beginning in the first quarter of 2027. That is the program by which the company will create a new class of nonvoting stock, a move it previously announced. The company expects to sell shares of its new “Class C” stock over time, though Meta said Monday it hasn’t finalized the arrangement.

One year ago, after Meta’s 3Q 2025 earnings, I wrote that the company was realizing the true cost of Reality Labs :

What I also think is happening is that Meta is finally paying the price for the billions of dollars it has spent on Reality Labs with precious little financial return to show for it. Yes, investors have long grumbled at how much money Meta has spent on AR and VR, but ultimately I think Zuckerberg has gotten a pass; even the stock market freakout in 2022 was more about TikTok and ATT than about the Metaverse (the Metaverse spending was taken as an indication that Meta’s core business was faltering).

This time, however, Zuckerberg once again seems to be asking for a blank check, and given that the last blank check is growing, not cashing, I think that investors are hesitant about writing another one. Again, I’m not sure this is necessarily fair — Meta is clearly leveraging more compute effectively in its ad business, and AI is not the Metaverse — but unless Zuckerberg wants to become the world’s biggest ad business salesman he’s going to need to show some tangible evidence sooner or later that Meta can in fact win on product.

What a difference a year makes. Meta has indeed shown up asking for that blank check, and just for context, this now-$97.5 billion worth of equity offerings very nearly matches all of Reality Labs’ recorded losses. Now, to be fair, those recorded losses only go back to Q4 2019; Meta bought Oculus for $2 billion in 2014, which is to say the cumulative losses since then are higher than the $100.8 billion on the books. Still, the fact we are in the same ballpark points to how much larger the AI expenditures are in aggregate.

What is different is that I strongly believe that Meta has earned the benefit of the doubt, and not just because I have been on the record since 2024 that Meta had arguably the largest AI opportunity ; rather, go back to what Zuckerberg wrote in July 2025 when Meta’s AI efforts seemed dead in the water, even as the company was spending millions of dollars on talent and making billions of dollars worth of compute commitments:

As profound as the abundance produced by AI may one day be, an even more meaningful impact on our lives will likely come from everyone having a personal superintelligence that helps you achieve your goals, create what you want to see in the world, experience any adventure, be a better friend to those you care about, and grow to become the person you aspire to be. Meta’s vision is to bring personal superintelligence to everyone. We believe in putting this power in people’s hands to direct it towards what they value in their own lives.

This is distinct from others in the industry who believe superintelligence should be directed centrally towards automating all valuable work, and then humanity will live on a dole of its output. At Meta, we believe that people pursuing their individual aspirations is how we have always made progress expanding prosperity, science, health, and culture. This will be increasingly important in the future as well. The intersection of technology and how people live is Meta’s focus, and this will only become more important in the future. If trends continue, then you’d expect people to spend less time in productivity software, and more time creating and connecting. Personal superintelligence that knows us deeply, understands our goals, and can help us achieve them will be by far the most useful.

It is difficult to overstate how important Muse is, not just in terms of what it represents in terms of AI , or the business opportunities , but specifically that it represents Zuckerberg delivering on his promise in a way that Reality Labs has never come close to doing. Yes, investors are grumbling about Meta’s spending plans and this equity raise, which is reasonable given that dilution is, as I noted yesterday , forcing existing shareholders to pay up. If Muse didn’t exist, however, and if it didn’t hew so closely to exactly what Zuckerberg promised he would build, I think there would be a revolt by the stock market.

---

Presented by

When I write about tech companies, I am often writing about businesses that depend on Stripe , because Stripe provides the foundation for Internet-native companies — including Stratechery.

Consider Substack: building Stratechery was complicated and involved gluing together disparate pieces; Substack made it easy by delivering an integrated offering. One piece that was the same, however, was Stripe: every Substack creator is also a Stripe customer, and that’s the case for many other creator platforms.

Of course, they didn’t succeed because of Stripe. Stripe doesn’t answer the hard questions about what to build or whether anyone will actually use it. But it does make more things practical to try.

---

Muse and the Frontier

From Artificial Analysis on X :

Announcing Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, featuring 2 new benchmarks and 3 upgrades. For the first time, the majority of the Index is built on private datasets.

The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is our composite measure of model capabilities across tasks reflecting real-world usage today. v5 is our biggest upgrade since v4 launched in January. With v5, 60% of the Index is now based on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers.

Alongside Intelligence Index v5, we’re launching the Artificial Analysis Progress Index v1, which tracks model capability over time on one continuous scale.

New benchmarks are, in my estimation, the only benchmarks worth paying attention to, because by virtue of being new, models have not been bench-maxxed, i.e. trained specifically to do well on the benchmarks in question. To that end, here is the Index :

The rankings here roughly match my sense of the landscape and, for what it is worth, my experience:

Opus 5.5 is the best model, although the GPT-6 family is very strong.

Chinese models are really not that close to the frontier (although Kimi K3.1 Pro’s showing is impressive; it’s also the largest Chinese model by far). This is obvious when you use them (which is to say that using them makes you very aware of what bench-maxxing means in practice).

Google and Meta are very much on the frontier, albeit not state-of-the-art (Grok, meanwhile, is falling far behind).

Meta’s comeback here is notable, and necessary: for all of the product sensibility that goes into Muse, it really does feel like the model is just barely good enough, which makes sense when you see Muse Spark Open’s score on this chart; you also realize why the release of Muse Wonder was an important milestone, and what a difference it is going to make when Meta figures out how to serve it efficiently to more users. Zuckerberg said on the earnings call :

And then there’s just continuing to increase the value in the product which I think we will largely do by continuing to develop new models. That’s why I mentioned that we launched Muse first on Muse Spark, and that’s what is currently the default across the free tier. And we rolled out Muse Wonder, and people can access that in the paid tier today. And we know that it performs a lot better, so we’re working on getting a more efficient version of Muse Wonder that we’ll be able to roll out more broadly. But you can imagine just as we iterate forward in two, three models into the future, when you have significantly higher intelligence and capability to solve many more problems for people and the ability to deliver that at a much more affordable price point, I think that that’s going to just unlock a lot more value to people. So we’re very excited about that.

Muse presents to investors a very binary question: if you think that it is a tremendous opportunity, then you must support Meta’s compute spending, because spending is the only way to get better models. That was, as I noted yesterday , the most important takeaway from Anthropic’s S-1: R&D compute is massively larger than inference compute, and its share of the total compute bill is growing. Yes, serving Muse will cost a lot; making Muse great will, at least for a while, cost more.

This also, I must admit, gave me more sympathy for Meta’s enterprise aspirations. The project is, to be clear, entirely solipsistic ; Zuckerberg said as much in his opening remarks:

One other note on compute economics is that since training is a large fixed cost, now that we have leading models, we want to serve as much high-margin inference demand as possible. That is why we are building the Meta Enterprise Platform, led by CJ Desai. Muse Wonder and even more advanced models that we are training can serve additional high-margin services beyond the Muse network, including our API, Muse Code, and other enterprise services.

What I mean by solipsistic is that the enterprise initiative is coming into being not because enterprise customers are asking for it, but because Zuckerberg sees the need to maximize the number of call options on the massive training costs he’s incurring. What makes me more sympathetic is that it is more likely than I thought that there will be enough inference compute to go around if this effort hits (just because the share of compute going to inference is likely lower than I originally thought). If I’m honest, I still think it’s an unnecessary distraction, but sometimes solipsism is self-preservation!

That noted, the most compelling argument for investors opposed to this spending is not that Muse doesn’t need it, but that Meta actually doesn’t need Muse. CFO Susan Li started out her summary of the company’s business results thusly:

Q3 Total Family of Apps revenue was $64.2 billion, up 26%. Q3 Family of Apps ad revenue was $63.1 billion, up 26% on both a reported and constant currency basis. In Q3, the tota...
